clinicalPearls: Characterised by effortful, halting speech with agrammatism and inconsistent speech-sound errors (apraxia of speech), while single-word comprehension is relatively preserved
It is the non-fluent/agrammatic variant of primary progressive aphasia and usually reflects underlying frontotemporal lobar degeneration with tau pathology
Comprehension of grammatically complex sentences is impaired, though understanding of individual words and object knowledge remains comparatively intact
Imaging typically shows atrophy and hypometabolism in the left posterior frontal and insular regions
Motor features overlapping with corticobasal syndrome or progressive supranuclear palsy may develop as the disease advances
Speech becomes progressively sparse and telegraphic, and some patients ultimately become mute
Distinguishing it from the semantic and logopenic variants relies on the pattern of speech production, grammar and repetition
reference.pathophysiology: Progressive non-fluent aphasia is the non-fluent/agrammatic variant of primary progressive aphasia, caused by neurodegeneration centred on the left inferior frontal, insular and premotor cortex that supports speech planning and grammatical processing. The most frequent underlying pathology is frontotemporal lobar degeneration associated with abnormal tau protein aggregation, and there is clinical and pathological overlap with corticobasal degeneration and progressive supranuclear palsy. Damage to these anterior language and motor-speech networks produces effortful, agrammatic output and apraxia of speech, with relative sparing of the temporal regions that store word meaning.
additionalInvestigations: Speech and language evaluation focusing on fluency, grammar and motor speech
MRI of the brain showing left posterior frontal and insular atrophy
Amyloid PET or cerebrospinal fluid biomarkers to exclude underlying Alzheimer pathology
Neuropsychological testing to document preserved single-word comprehension and object knowledge
Assessment for parkinsonian and corticobasal features over time
redFlags: Emerging parkinsonism, limb apraxia or gaze palsy suggesting corticobasal or supranuclear palsy overlap
Rapid progression suggesting an alternative aggressive pathology
Dysphagia and aspiration risk as bulbar and motor features advance
Progression to mutism with loss of functional communication
reference.prognosis: The disorder progresses over years, with speech becoming increasingly sparse and eventual mutism in many patients, and frequent evolution of motor features; prognosis depends on the underlying pathology, and management is supportive with speech and language therapy and communication aids.
pitfalls: Confusing agrammatic non-fluent output with the anomia and word-retrieval failure of the logopenic variant
Overlooking apraxia of speech as a defining feature
Assuming Alzheimer pathology when frontotemporal lobar degeneration is more likely
Missing evolving corticobasal or supranuclear palsy features
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: No disease-modifying drug exists; management centres on speech and language therapy targeting motor speech, grammar and functional communication strategies
Communication aids and augmentative and alternative communication as speech becomes sparse and in anticipation of eventual mutism
Treat associated neuropsychiatric symptoms such as depression, apathy and behavioural change with appropriate supportive and pharmacological measures
Monitor for and manage emerging parkinsonian, corticobasal or supranuclear palsy motor features, with falls prevention, physiotherapy and swallowing assessment
Dysphagia surveillance and nutritional support as bulbar and motor involvement develops
Multidisciplinary support across neurology, speech and language therapy, occupational therapy and dietetics, with caregiver education and advance care planning
